title: where dharma is, there is victory
hookLine: the Pandavas walk toward the mother whose sons they killed, and she has the power to burn them
carry: yato dharmas tato jayah: where dharma is, victory is
tomorrow: what does Gandhari see when she finally looks?

cards: The winners of the war have a visit to make, and nobody wants to make it. The five Pandava brothers, with Krishna beside them, have to stand in front of Gandhari, the queen whose sons fell to them on that field.
She has kept her eyes bound with a cloth for her whole married life, the story says, and her years of discipline have given her a power the brothers fear. Her anger could burn.
Before they arrive, the sage Vyasa comes to her first.

teach.h: WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY
teach.b: Vyasa reminds Gandhari of her own words. All through the war, when Duryodhana came asking for her blessing, she gave him the same answer: where dharma is, there victory is. She never blessed him with victory.
Now, Vyasa says, the words have come true. Don't let anger undo them.

So she holds the curse back, but she has a question for Bhima. Why did you strike my son below the navel, against the rules of the mace fight? Bhima admits he was afraid, and reminds her what her son did to Draupadi.
Then Gandhari asks for the king. Yudhishthira comes forward, trembling, hands joined: I killed your sons. Curse me.
But through a small gap in the cloth, her gaze falls on the tips of his toes, and his nails turn dark and damaged. Arjuna, watching, steps behind Krishna.
Then her anger passes, and she sends them to their own mother, Kunti. One glance, and that's all the burning there is.

Now hold on to her words: yato dharmas tato jayah, where dharma is, there is victory. She said them to her own son, and wouldn't bend them for him. Hindus still live by that line; it's the motto of India's Supreme Court.
The teaching: you don't bless your own side. You bless what's right, and trust victory to follow it. Today, when someone you love asks you to take their side, that's Gandhari's test.

how: Gandhari's answer to her son, yato dharmas tato jayah, where dharma is, there is victory, is quoted across India and is the motto of the Supreme Court of India; storytellers and dance-dramas return to her meeting with the Pandavas.

o: woman: the book where the epic's women speak
a vow of silence kept by a grieving widow
the blindfold a queen ties over her eyes

games.q: Gandhari meets the Pandavas — tap the pairs.
p: reminds her of her own words

s: Gandhari blessed Duryodhana to win the war
she told him, where dharma is, there victory is.
a glance through her blindfold marked Yudhishthira's toenails
her gaze fell on the tips of his toes through a gap in the cloth, and the nails turned dark.
Gandhari burned the Pandavas with a curse that day
her anger passed, and she sent them on to Kunti.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. the mother of every son you killed is waiting, and her anger can burn. what do you do?
o: send Krishna in to speak for you.
stand before her and say, curse me.
wait until her grief has cooled.
games.why: he comes forward, trembling, hands joined, admits he killed her sons and asks her to curse him. holding to her own words about dharma, she doesn't.

practice: Close your eyes, the way Gandhari's were closed, and bring back a moment when someone close to you wanted you on their side, and you could have said the thing that burned.
Breathe in and feel the heat; breathe out and rest in the space between the heat and the words. If you pray, you can ask, as Gandhari did, not for your side to win, but for dharma.
If you don't, just rest in that space a little longer.

wordCard.voice: Stri. Woman, and the name of the Mahabharata book where the women of both sides finally speak. Today it's Gandhari, holding to dharma over her own son.

orig.note: dharma: in Gandhari's answer to her son, where dharma is, there victory is.

carryVoice: Your line: yato dharmas tato jayah, where dharma is, victory is. Tomorrow, Gandhari is given eyes to see the whole field. Day eight hundred fifty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Stri Parva, Vyasa's counsel to Gandhari, her questions to Bhima, and her meeting with Yudhishthira
'Yato dharmas tato jayah', motto of the Supreme Court of India
